generatedProse.concept-context: In any subject, the words you search with decide what you find. A search begins with an objective, a clear statement of what you need, and a thought about the sort of evidence that would answer it. It then turns into keywords: the terms that capture the topic. Because one idea can be named in several ways, synonyms matter, and adding them broadens the search so you do not miss relevant work.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two students plan a search on the same topic: whether working in groups helps students learn.

{{learner-a}} types the sentence 'does working in groups help students learn' straight into the search box. The results are thin and off-topic. {{learner-a}} has not set an objective or chosen keywords: the whole question has gone in as one long phrase, so the tool struggles to match it. This is searching without a plan.

{{learner-b}} first sets the objective, recent evidence on group work and learning, then picks keywords: 'group work', 'students' and 'learning'. Noticing that 'students' could also be 'learners', she adds that synonym to catch more work. Her search returns relevant material. This is a planned search with well-chosen keywords.

Both students searched the same topic. Only {{learner-b}} planned the search and chose keywords, with a synonym to broaden it.
generatedProse.summary: A search begins with a plan: an objective, and a thought about what sort of evidence you need and how recent it should be. The plan becomes keywords, the terms that drive the search, and synonyms such as 'learners' for 'students' broaden it so you catch the same idea under different words. You can now plan a simple search, identify keywords, and give a synonym to widen your results. With this, you are ready to search on purpose.

check.body: In the worked example, what did {{learner-b}} do that made the search work?

items.text: She set an objective and chose keywords, adding a synonym to broaden the search.
She typed the whole question into the search box as one long phrase.
She searched for the single longest word she could think of.
She avoided using any synonyms to keep the search narrow.

feedback.correct: That's right. A clear objective plus well-chosen keywords and a synonym is what worked.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for what {{learner-b}} DID: objective, keywords and a synonym.
feedback.incorrectFinal: {{learner-b}} set an objective and chose keywords, adding a synonym. Typing the whole question, chasing long words, or avoiding synonyms are what weakens a search.

_prompts.concept-context: What does this look like in practice within the given context? Write a short follow-on from the generic definition above, in the learner's own subject or discipline. Keep it to two or three sentences, mid-register, following straight on from the generic definition.
_prompts.worked-example: Give a subject-specific worked example of this lesson's concept: a weaker or less-developed version first, then a stronger version reached by better practice, using the context cast (character tokens) consistently. Keep the weaker-then-stronger shape and the two-part contrast; carry the cast only through the {{learner-a}} (weaker) and {{learner-b}} (stronger) tokens, never a literal name (the pack supplies the whole body, but not the names). Each example paragraph must begin with its token, weaker first - merge-context.js's wrapProse() only emits the we-weaker/we-stronger cue classes for a paragraph that leads with the token. The merge renders it as a block quote, so write it as continuous prose, not as a quoted comment plus commentary.
_prompts.summary: Recap what the learner can now do, in terms of their own subject or context. One short paragraph. Do not restate the learning outcomes verbatim.
_prompts.check: Write the subject's own version of this lesson's check question(s), testing the same outcome in the learner's own discipline. Keep the same number of items and the same correctness pattern as the generic version; reword the stem and items for the subject. Keep the component-level feedback (correct / notFinal / final) teaching, never a bare verdict.
